identification.summary: Storm-1747 is Microsoft's designation for the actor that develops, supports and advertises the Tycoon2FA adversary-in-the-middle (AiTM) phishing-as-a-service (PhaaS) platform [S1]. Microsoft says Tycoon2FA consistently was the most prolific PhaaS platform it observed throughout 2025 [S5]. The actor is a financially motivated cybercrime service operator, not a state-linked group, in the sources reviewed [S1][S4].
identification.notes: Microsoft states Tycoon2FA emerged in August 2023 [S1]. Microsoft names the actor Storm-1747 (a group in development) and the tool Tycoon2FA; Microsoft's Defender XDR threat analytics carries an actor profile (Storm-1747), a tool profile (Tycoon2FA) and a technique profile (AiTM credential phishing) [S1]. Do not conflate Storm-1747 (kit operator) with the customers who run campaigns using the kit; Microsoft notes the panel has no built-in mailer, so distribution is the customers' job [S1]. Some researchers have speculated about a link to the Salty2FA framework; this is speculation in secondary reporting and is not verified here [S10].

attribution.sponsor: Financially motivated criminal PhaaS operator; no state sponsor identified in cited sources
attribution.confidence: Microsoft attributes development, support and advertising of Tycoon2FA to Storm-1747 [S1]. Microsoft's blog names no individuals, location or operator Telegram handles [S1]. No arrests of operators were reported in the sources reviewed [S7].
attribution.basis: Microsoft Threat Intelligence and Digital Crimes Unit analysis, plus a civil action in the US District Court for the Southern District of New York to seize 330 domains, reported by secondary outlets [S1][S4]. The kit was sold via Telegram and Signal [S1].

objectives: Financial gain from selling panel access to Tycoon2FA, reported at about USD 350 per month [S1]. Customers use the kit to steal credentials and session cookies, and follow-on activity observed by Microsoft includes mailbox rule creation, registering new authenticator apps, and launching further phishing from compromised accounts; Microsoft also lists reverting unauthorized payroll or direct-deposit changes in its remediation steps [S1].

targeting.notes: Microsoft says campaigns reached over 500,000 organizations worldwide and tens of millions of messages per month, hitting education, healthcare, finance, non-profit, government and nearly all other sectors [S1]. Lures impersonate Microsoft 365, OneDrive, Outlook, SharePoint, Gmail, Azure, Okta and DocuSign [S1]. Reporting on the Microsoft case says more than 100 HealthISAC members were successfully phished and that at least two New York hospitals, six municipal schools and three universities faced attempted or successful compromise [S11]. Proofpoint data reported by ITPro ordered targets as technology, financial services, business services, manufacturing, healthcare and government, and counted over 3 million messages in February 2026 [S11]. Targets are customer-selected, so victimology reflects the customer base and not a single tasking [S1].

capabilities.summary: Tycoon2FA is an AiTM reverse proxy that relays credentials and MFA codes to the real service and steals session cookies, bypassing SMS, one-time-passcode and push-based MFA; stolen sessions can remain usable after a password reset unless sessions and tokens are revoked [S1]. Each customer gets a per-user web panel for lure templates, branding, redirect routing, CAPTCHA settings, attachment generation, victim tracking and exfiltration (to the panel and/or a Telegram bot) [S1]. Lure delivery uses PDF/DOCX with QR codes, SVG files with embedded redirect logic, HTML attachments, EML, and redirect links, sometimes sent from compromised accounts within existing threads [S1]. Evasion includes custom regenerated HTML5-canvas CAPTCHAs (earlier Cloudflare Turnstile), browser fingerprinting, datacenter-IP and geo filtering, detection of PhantomJS and Burp Suite, blocking of dev-tool shortcuts, Base64/Base91 and invisible-Unicode obfuscation, decoy redirects, and redirect chains through Azure Blob Storage, Firebase, Wix, TikTok and Google resources [S1]. Infrastructure is mostly on Cloudflare (including Workers URLs) with campaign FQDNs living about 24-72 hours and automated subdomain rotation; TLD use shifted from .es/.ru toward cheap generic TLDs, and subdomain naming moved from high-entropy strings (July 2025) to readable service-themed words (December 2025) [S1]. Bridewell reports proxied OAuth consent screens can yield refresh tokens that survive password resets [S9]. Cyfirma reports bypass of SMS, TOTP and push MFA [S8].

campaigns.name: Tycoon2FA emerges
campaigns.summary: Microsoft states Tycoon2FA appeared in August 2023 and became one of the most widespread PhaaS platforms [S1]. Early campaigns favored .es and .ru domains and Cloudflare Turnstile as the main CAPTCHA [S1].

campaigns.name: High-entropy subdomain rotation
campaigns.summary: Microsoft observed algorithmically generated high-entropy subdomains in use in July 2025 [S1].

campaigns.name: Peak volume observed by Microsoft
campaigns.summary: Microsoft Threat Intelligence stated Tycoon2FA was the most prolific PhaaS it observed in 2025 and that Defender for Office 365 blocked more than 13 million malicious emails linked to it in October 2025 [S5].

campaigns.name: Shift to readable service-themed subdomains
campaigns.summary: Subdomains moved to readable words tied to workflows or services such as cloud, azure, microsoft, sharepoint and onedrive; the kit also shifted to rotating custom CAPTCHAs [S1].

campaigns.name: Microsoft/Europol-led disruption
campaigns.summary: Microsoft's Digital Crimes Unit, Europol and industry partners disrupted Tycoon2FA; Microsoft obtained a court order from the US District Court for the Southern District of New York to seize 330 domains used for core infrastructure including control panels and fake login pages [S1][S4]. Reporting cites more than 96,000 distinct phishing victims, including more than 55,000 Microsoft customers, and authorities from six countries and 11 security firms or organizations [S4]. Cloudflare says it took down Workers projects and infrastructure supporting the kit, coordinated with Microsoft's civil case [S6]. Europol-led reporting also cites about 64,000 campaigns and about 2,000 users [S5][S11].

campaigns.name: Reported resumption after disruption
campaigns.summary: The Cloud Security Alliance research note (2026-03-26) reports the platform survived the disruption and returned; OODA Loop and CybersecurityNews headlines likewise report operators resuming activity [S7][S12]. Figures such as volumes returning within days and no operator arrests come from secondary summaries and were not verified against primary documents [S7].

diamond.adversary: Storm-1747, a criminal PhaaS developer/operator that sells panel access via Telegram and Signal; no named individuals in Microsoft's report [S1]. Customers are separate actors who run campaigns [S1].
diamond.capability: AiTM reverse-proxy kit with per-customer panel, MFA relay and session-cookie theft, multi-format lures, anti-analysis and CAPTCHA gating, and Telegram-bot exfiltration [S1].
diamond.infrastructure: Cloudflare-hosted, short-lived (24-72 h) rotating subdomains on cheap generic TLDs, redirect chains via legitimate cloud services, Telegram bots for exfiltration; 330 core domains seized in March 2026 [S1][S4][S6].
diamond.victim: Cloud email/identity accounts (Microsoft 365, Google) at organizations globally, notably education, healthcare, finance, non-profit and government [S1][S11].
diamond.socioPolitical: Cybercrime-as-a-service economy: Microsoft links Tycoon2FA's rise to disruptions of other PhaaS platforms (Caffeine, RaccoonO365) and the DCU has pursued a series of such takedowns [S1][S2]. No state tasking is indicated in sources.
diamond.technology: Microsoft 365/Entra ID and Google sign-in flows, session cookies and OAuth tokens, Cloudflare Workers, Telegram and Signal, QR/SVG/PDF/HTML attachments [S1][S9].

gaps: Identity, location and organization of the Storm-1747 operators are not given in Microsoft's report and were not found in other sources [S1].
Microsoft's On the Issues post and the court filing were seen only in search results; the full text could not be opened, so case details rely on secondary coverage [S2][S4].
Reported post-takedown resumption and volume figures come from secondary summaries; no primary vendor telemetry was reviewed, and the current operating status is unknown [S7].
The Salty2FA link is speculation in secondary reporting and is unverified [S10].

Target counts differ across sources (Microsoft 500,000 organizations; 96,000 victims in court-related coverage; 64,000 campaigns and 2,000 users in Europol-led coverage) and use different methods [S1][S4][S5][S11].
Several vendor reports (Cyfirma, Bridewell, Elastic, Okta, Proofpoint) could not be opened directly; their content is taken from search summaries.
Malpedia and MITRE ATT&CK group mapping for Storm-1747 was not verified; the actor record has no MITRE group id.

implications.jipoe: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. Step 1 (battlespace): the relevant terrain is cloud identity (Microsoft 365/Entra ID, Google) and email, not military networks; the service is sold commercially, so any DoD-affiliated or contractor mailbox is a potential customer-chosen victim [S1][S11]. Step 2 (effects): stolen session tokens bypass common MFA and persist past password resets, enabling mailbox access, inbox rules and onward phishing from trusted accounts [S1]. Step 3 (adversary): a commercial enabler, not a tasked force; capability is lowered to any paying customer, so intent varies by customer and could include state-aligned buyers (not shown in sources) [S1]. Step 4 MLCOA: customers send QR-code, SVG or HTML lures from compromised threads to harvest tokens, then run BEC or further phishing [S1]. MDCOA (analyst inference): the kit rebrands or migrates to competing platforms after takedown and retargets cleared personnel and defense suppliers; reporting indicates the platform resumed after the March 2026 disruption [S7]. Candidate indicators: short-lived Cloudflare Workers/subdomains on cheap TLDs, URLs ending in an email placeholder, risky browser sign-ins from unmanaged devices following email URL clicks, new authenticator registrations, and unexpected inbox rules [S1].
implications.jcc2: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. Situational awareness: track token-theft alerts (AiTM sign-in, stolen-session-cookie use) and Microsoft threat analytics for Storm-1747 and Tycoon2FA across Defender and cloud identity telemetry [S1]. Authorities: response actions such as session and token revocation, MFA re-registration and mailbox-rule removal are identity and email administration actions that need the system owner's approval; the domain seizure here was a civil court action by Microsoft, so no DoD authority is implied [S1][S4]. Mission assurance: enforce phishing-resistant MFA (FIDO2, Windows Hello for Business, passkeys) and authentication-strength Conditional Access for privileged roles, since OTP and push MFA are bypassed [S1]. Coordination: share indicators with the cloud provider and the owning network defenders, and coordinate with the provider's Digital Crimes Unit channels, noting the healthcare sector's HealthISAC participation as a model for sector sharing [S1][S11].
